notes.meaning: In this vision, God's Spirit carried Ezekiel to the east gate of the temple court. There he saw twenty-five leaders of the people gathered in council. Two of them, Jaazaniah and Pelatiah, were singled out by name because they held great influence in Jerusalem.

The Lord told Ezekiel that these rulers were plotting wickedness and giving bad advice to the city. Instead of urging the people to repent, they encouraged them to rebel against Babylon and ignore God's prophets.

These leaders told the people that judgment was far away, so it was safe to settle down and build houses in Jerusalem. They used a proverb, comparing the city to a bronze cooking pot and themselves to meat inside. They foolishly believed the city's thick stone walls would shield them from the fire of war.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Catholic Douay-Rheims translation reads this as a statement that houses were recently built, which the leaders took as proof that the city would not be destroyed.

notes.meaning: God commanded Ezekiel to speak out boldly against these deceitful leaders. Repeating the command showed how urgent it was to shatter their false sense of safety.
The Spirit of the Lord came with power upon Ezekiel and gave him the exact words to speak. God warned the rulers that he knew every thought, plan, and secret motive in their minds.

God accused the leaders of filling Jerusalem with murdered victims. They were guilty of shedding innocent blood through unjust courts and greedy oppression. They were also responsible for the deaths caused by their foolish choice to fight Babylon.

God took their own cooking-pot picture and turned it back on them. He said the only meat staying inside the pot was the bodies of the victims they had killed. The proud rulers who thought they were safe would be dragged out of the city.

These leaders feared dying by the enemy's sword, so they made alliances and defended the city to avoid it. Yet God declared that the very weapon they dreaded would be brought against them because of their sins.
God promised to take them out of their fortified city and hand them over to foreign conquerors. All their plans to escape would fail as God carried out his judgment through the Babylonian army.

The rulers would be killed by the sword not inside Jerusalem, but at the border of the land of Israel. This was fulfilled when Babylon's king put the leaders to death at Riblah on Israel's northern frontier. By this judgment, they would finally know that the Lord is God.
The city would not protect them like a cooking pot, nor would they be safe like meat inside it. God repeated that their punishment would take place on the outer borders of Israel.

This punishment fell upon them because they had cast aside God's rules and lived just like the pagan nations around them. Since they refused to learn who God was through obedience to his word, they would learn it through his punishment.

While Ezekiel was speaking this prophecy in his vision, Pelatiah suddenly died. This sudden death was a guarantee that the rest of the message would soon come true. Shaken by the sight, Ezekiel fell on his face and begged God not to wipe out the small remnant of Israel that was left.

God answered Ezekiel's cry by pointing him toward his fellow captives in Babylon. The people remaining in Jerusalem were scorning the exiles, claiming they were cut off from God and had lost their right to the land. But God revealed that the despised exiles were his true people.

God admitted that he had scattered the exiles into distant lands, but he promised to be a sanctuary, or holy dwelling place, for them while they were there. Even without the stone temple in Jerusalem, the captives would have real fellowship with God wherever they were.
God promised that their exile would come to an end. He would gather them back from the foreign countries where they had been scattered and return the land of Israel to them.
When the people returned home, they would clear away all the hateful idols that had polluted the land. The painful discipline of captivity would finally cure them of worshiping false gods.

God promised to renew them from the inside out by giving them a single, undivided heart and putting a new spirit within them. He would take away their hard, stubborn heart of stone and give them a soft heart of flesh that listens and responds to him.

This change of heart would lead them to obey God's laws gladly in everyday life. In this way, God's sacred covenant relationship would be restored: they would truly be his people, and he would be their God.
God warned that those who still loved and chased after repulsive idols would not share in these blessings. He would bring justice down upon them and punish them according to their evil conduct.
The winged cherubim spread their wings to fly, accompanied by the spinning wheels at their sides. High above them rested the shining glory of the God of Israel.

The glory of the Lord rose up from within Jerusalem and came to rest on the Mount of Olives just east of the city. Moving away step by step showed God's patience, but it also showed that he had officially withdrawn his protection from the city and temple.

The Spirit brought Ezekiel back to the Jewish captives in Babylonia, and the heavenly vision ended. Ezekiel then faithfully told the exiles everything the Lord had revealed, showing them that the city they left behind was doomed and that their true hope lay in God's promises for the future.
